title: Tape a drywall crack: lay paper joint tape centered along it and bed it in the wet compound with a joint knife
instruction: Tape the crack in the wall panel with the paper tape and the joint knife, then lay the knife back on the bench.
context: Hairline cracks that radiate from the corners of doors and windows are a common sight in homes, and taping one with paper tape and joint compound is the standard repair in home-repair guides (Family Handyman). The tape makers' order is: lay a layer of joint compound along the crack, center the tape on it, embed it while the compound is wet, and take off the excess with a broad knife, leaving about 1/32 in. of compound under the tape. Tape off the line, a starved stretch with too little compound under it, a stretch never pressed in, wrinkles and torn tape are what the result is checked for. Finishers set the tape first, pulled tight and lightly pressed onto the wet bed with the fingers, which holds it in place, then embed it with the knife.
setup: Positions are in cm from the midpoint between the two arm bases, with x forward, y to the robot's left and the table top at z 0. Panel: an offcut of half-inch (12.7 mm) drywall, 40 x 40 cm, paper face toward the robot, leaning back 20 degrees from vertical; the face's bottom edge rests on the table at x 37.0, from y -24.0 to 16.0, against a pine 1x2 stop strip, with a pine 2x2 brace behind and two drywall screws into it (fixed). Crack: a 12 cm crack in the face running straight up it: bottom end at (42.3, -2.0, 15.0), top end at (46.4, -2.0, 26.3). Bed: wet ready-mixed joint compound, 3 mm (1/8 in.) deep and 10 cm wide, centered on the crack, from 9 cm below its middle to 9 cm above it along its line. Pencil ticks (carpenter's pencil or marker) on the crack's line 2 cm past each end of the bed mark where the crack runs, since the bed hides it. Tape: an 18.8 cm strip of 2-1/16 in. (52.4 mm) paper joint tape, 0.215 mm thick, 1.4 g, lying flat on a 2x4 offcut (38 x 89 mm, 30 cm long) standing on edge on a scrap of 3/4 in. plywood (top 10.8 cm above the table) on the bench to the left; the tape runs from its top end at (18.0, 30.0, 10.8) away from the robot and to the left (30 degrees left of straight ahead), its top end 3.5 cm past the offcut's end. Knife: a 4 in. flexible joint knife, steel blade 102 mm wide at the edge and 76 mm long, blue plastic handle 115 x 30 x 22 mm, 110 g, lying flat on the bench to the right, blade to the left, the blade's root at (20.0, -23.0). Both arms start at their ready pose. Real rig: one ready-mixed all-purpose joint compound from a single tub (ProForm All Purpose Ready Mix) and ProForm 2-1/16 in. paper joint tape; the compound is spread along the crack with the knife and struck off level with two 1/8 in. (3 mm) hardboard rails laid with their inner edges 50 mm either side of the crack (10 mm inside the pencil lines), from 2 cm inside one tick to 2 cm inside the other, then the rails are lifted away. Each of the four gripper fingers wears a disposable nitrile glove (size L): a YAM finger is about 6.8 cm wide, too wide for a glove's finger, so the finger goes into the glove's palm and the glove's fingers are folded back over the finger's outer face and taped there with the cuff by two turns of painter's tape; every press and grip on the tape and the knife happens through the glove. A plastic drop sheet lies under the stand, the tape block and the knife's spot; the compound is water-based and wipes off with a damp sponge. The knife's blade is wiped clean before it is laid back, so the handle the gripper takes stays clean.
scoring: Real trial, judged by eye from the overhead video, an approximation of the simulated rules below (two pencil lines are drawn parallel to the crack 60 mm either side of it, outside the bed, once when the offcut is prepared, before any bed is laid and before any trial). 0.25: the tape covers the crack end to end (on the ticks' line, its ends within 3 cm of the bed's ends) and the knife, held, is drawn down over at least half of it. 0.5: and centered: along the crack the gap from each tape edge to its pencil line looks the same on both sides (about 34 mm each; tape 3 mm off center leaves 31 and 37 mm). 0.75: and after the pass compound shows squeezed out along both edges of the tape over the crack, the tape lies flat with no bubble or loose edge, and no arm touches the tape after the pass (a starved stretch or one never pressed shows no squeeze-out). 1.0: and no wrinkle or tear, the knife laid on the bench and released, and hands off. Torn tape caps the score at 0.5; doing nothing scores 0. A hand may hold the tape's top end and fingers may press the tape onto the bed before the knife; no part of an arm may touch bedded tape over the crack. In simulation the same outcomes are measured through the compound model (per-station depth). The crack is checked at 13 stations, one every 1 cm from end to end. 0.25: the tape lies on the face over the crack end to end (at every station the crack is under a strip of tape on the face) and the held knife has been drawn over it, pressing it, at half the stations or more; tape set by hand alone scores 0. 0.5: and centered: its center line within 3 mm of the crack at every station. 0.75: and bedded at 90% of the stations: 0.4 to 1.6 mm of compound under it on the crack and 18 mm either side of its center line (the makers' sheets: about 1/32 in., 0.7-0.8 mm), compound squeezed out at both edges, bonded, and no part of either arm touched it there once it was bedded. 1.0: and no wrinkle (every strip over the crack flat on the face, all its corners within 0.7 mm), the knife set down (released, every arm link at least 2 mm from it, on the bench, every part at least 2 mm clear of the face), no part of either arm on the tape (every link's collision hulls checked), and the knife and tape still (under 1 cm/s, the knife turning under 0.5 degree per step), for 1 s. Torn tape (the knife pressing with one corner, its edge turned more than 15 degrees out of the face, dragged 5 mm or more along the tape) caps the score at 0.5. Doing nothing scores 0. Possible scores: 0, 0.25, 0.5, 0.75, 1.0. Bedding: a knife held by a hand and sliding at least 1 cm/s, which the physics engine (PhysX contact reporting) reports touching a strip of tape lying on the face while its total contact force on the tape, normal to the face, is at least 2 N, presses the compound under it to a depth set by the blade's angle to the face: 0.8 mm at 40 degrees or less, 0.1 mm at 60 degrees or more, linear between (an assumed law, set to the makers' 1/32 in.); the rest squeezes out to the nearer edge. A strip bedded with 0.4-1.6 mm left bonds (wet compound holds it; a peel lifts it off, and sliding it more than a few millimeters undoes the bedding). Fingers, a dab, a still knife or a knife with no hand on it bed nothing. Tack: a strip in contact with a fingertip while it lies on the face over compound sticks weakly (its sliding slowed to under 1 mm a minute; a 2 mm lift peels it); tack is never counted as bedded. The force needed is estimated from plastic squeeze flow of the compound out from under the 52 mm tape through the 0.8 mm film: about 1 N at the 200 Pa yield stress of a commercially available joint compound (US 12,054,627 B2): about 1 N is the estimate of what bedding needs, and the rule asks for twice that, 2 N, a conservative margin. A knife near the tape but not touching it, or touching it with less force, beds nothing; at or above 2 N the film left is set by the angle alone.
reset_notes: Each real trial (reset about 3 minutes): the same offcut is reused: the used tape is peeled off, the compound scraped off the face with the knife and the face wiped with a damp sponge (replace the offcut when its face paper scuffs; a 4 x 8 ft sheet gives 18); a new 3 mm bed from the same tub (about 60 mL, 1/4 cup, used unthinned at room temperature, 20-25 C, stirred with the knife first, the lid kept on between trials) is struck off between the two hardboard rails just before the trial, which starts within 2 minutes while it is wet; a new 18.8 cm strip of tape is laid on the 2x4 offcut as at the start, its top end 3.5 cm past the 2x4's end and its bottom end on a pencil tick on the 2x4 (the 2x4 and the knife go back to painter's-tape outlines on the bench); the knife's blade is wiped and the knife laid back; the gloves and drop sheet are wiped with a damp sponge (a torn glove is replaced). Per trial only one strip of tape and about 60 mL (1/4 cup) of compound are used. The pencil ticks and the two pencil lines are drawn once, when the offcut is prepared, and stay outside the bed. In simulation every trial starts with the fresh bed, the tape on the offcut and every bond and tack off.
fidelity: Tape: 28 rigid hinged strips with the real width, weight and bending stiffness, contact boxes 1 mm thick. Compound: a 1 mm height field; the knife's angle sets the film left, the rest squeezes out. Bedding needs 2 N of knife contact force on the tape (PhysX), twice the estimated 1 N. Knife and tape use 128 solver position iterations (a 0.05 g strip under the 110 g knife does not converge at the default); masses unchanged. A bedded strip's hold is a joint released by a peel or slide.
scores: Dream-1 run: 0 (2,400 steps: its hands went to the tape and the knife but carried neither to the panel; the tape stayed on its block); demo: 1.0 (1,980 steps, 99 s)
